lines.text: Last time, Jev read a million letters, and sent the hard ones to people.
But most letters don't just need sorting. They need an answer, written back.
And Jev can't write. That's the whole point of it.
Our trains can. They lay down a reply one word at a time. But every word costs time, and money.
So picture a signal box at the junction. Every letter stops here first.
Inside, Jev reads it in one pass, and sets the points.
Letters it's sure about take the short line. Sorted, answered from a template, done.
The unsure ones take the long line, to a train that can read slowly, and write back.
Here's the puzzle. By TypeSafe's own tests, Jev is up to four hundred and forty-four times cheaper than a chatbot.
Say Jev sends one letter in five on to the train. How much cheaper is the whole system, than using the train for everything? Take a guess.
Four hundred times? Not even close. About five.
Let's run a thousand letters through the box.
Eight hundred take the short line. Each one costs almost nothing.
Two hundred take the long line. And each of those costs a full train ride.
Now count the coins. Nearly all of them were spent on the long line.
Written as math: one letter costs Jev's price, plus the share that rides the train, times the train's price.
Divide by the train's price. Jev's part is one over four hundred and forty-four. Almost nothing. What's left is the share: one in five.
So the whole system costs about a fifth of the train. Five times cheaper.
The four hundred and forty-four barely matters. What matters is how many letters Jev keeps off the train.
Time works the same way. Fast answers for most letters, slow ones only where they're needed.
Send one in ten, and it's about ten times cheaper. One in a hundred, about eighty.
But only letters Jev is truly sure about should stay off the train. And sure only counts if the number is honest.
If Jev is overconfident, a hard letter takes the short line, and nobody writes the careful answer it needed.
So the two aren't rivals. One decides, fast. The other writes, carefully.
TypeSafe calls Jev a System One model. Fast. The trains are the slow System Two.
And the signal box sends each letter to the kind of thinking it needs.
But there's a catch. A number that's honest on one kind of letter can drift on another. So before you trust it, check it on your own letters.
Let's go back to where we started. Ask a chatbot the same question twice, and you might get two different answers.
That's not a glitch. It's how they write: one word at a time, and every word is a small bet.
Jev makes a different bargain. It never writes. It answers a fixed question, in one pass, with a number.
And a number is something you can do math with. You can price it, draw a line, and decide who reads what.
But only if it's honest. Ninety-one percent has to mean right about ninety-one times in a hundred.
So the future probably isn't one machine that does everything. It's a signal box. Fast numbers where they're enough, careful words where they're needed, and people where it matters most.
The model that doesn't talk may end up deciding who should.
